The year whose history is the subject of the present report has 
been unprecedented, as far as regards the outward success of our 
Association, and we hope has been blessed greatly to many who have 
in various ways come under the influence of its agencics. The 
report is divided according to the departments of the various Stand- 
ing Committees, with the addition of special sections for the Conven- 
tion held in our city in the month of June, and the efforts of our 
members in the formation of new Associations. 


COMMITTEE ON MEMBERSHIP ROOMS AND LIBRARY. 
MEMBERSHIP. 


During the year there have been 249 new members added to 
our rolls, of which number there were 13 honorary, 97 active, 139 
associate, and 6 have become life members, making a nominal total 
of 649 members altogether. The Committee have not completed 
the revisal of the list, with which work they were entrusted at the 
beginning of the year, and therefore they are uncertain how many 
names would have to be struck from the above numbers to show the 
really efficient foree of our membership. They recommend to 
their successors the speedy prosecution of this work. The large 
additions made to the numbers are principally owing to the great 
activity of our members about the time of the Convention, and prin- 
cipally of one who devoted much time to an active canvas. We must 
not forget, however, the active personal interest in the matter taken 
by many of our pastors and influential friends. 

Karly in the year corresponding members of this Committee were 
appointed in all the congregations with which our members are connect- 
ed, and efforts were made through them to increase the membership and 
collect the annual fees. The latter work, unfortunately always difficult, 
was in a very incomplete state till the close of the summer, when it was 
found advisable to put the matter in the hands of a regular collector, 
who has since, with much difficulty, collected about $120 out of $375 
then due. No fact could show more elearly the need of a revisal of 
the roll. 


4 


It has been very noticeable that many of our members who are 
not remiss in paying their subscriptions do not take the first step 
towards a real connection with the Society, by being present at its 
meetings. Partially to cure this evil the plan of sending to every 
newly elected member a copy of the constitution, and with it an 
invitation to be present at the Rooms on a certain evening, when he 
might be introduced to members present, has been adopted with very 
good success, so far as time has allowed of its being tested. 


ROOMS. 


The Association ‘still occupies the second flat of the Bible- 
house, with the use of the large Committee room in the third flat. 
The Reading Room, which is now very attractive, has been used 
much more freely than in any former year. In March last the ceil- 
ings were decorated, and other additions were made to the beauty 
and comfort of the Rooms, in great measure, at the expense of the 
Secretary and his brother. The new elegant tables and chairs have 
proved much more convenient than the furniture they supplanted, 
Note should also be taken of donations from Mr. T. Jas. Claxton of 
a new stair carpet, which, we scarcely regret to say, is already, in 
four months, used up, and hearth rugs; from Mr. Chas. Storer of 
two gilt signs for the door; from Messrs. D. & J. Tees, of labour on 
wash-room; and from a sister Association in Bristol, U.S., of a 
photograph of its rooms. The system adopted two years ago by Mr. 
Sandham for supplying the Reading Room tables has been success- 
fully carried out by him this year. The Association is now in receipt 
of twenty weekly, one tri-weekly and five daily papers, and six 
yearly, six quarterly, and twenty-eight monthly periodicals, making 
in all eighty-five, all of which are procured free of charge, with the 
exception of three papers. In this connection we have to thank the 
publishers of the New York Albion and the (London) Christian 
World for adding their papers to our stock. 


LIBRARY. 


The number of volumes issued during the year has been 1,423 
from the Circulating Library, while the works of reference have been 
constantly in use. The number of those who have taken out books 
has been 230. The Committee of the Association would acknow- 
ledge with thanks the following donations of books :—Mr. Alfred 
Sandham, 19 volumes; W.K. Bessy, M.D., 6 do; EH. H. Trenholme, 
M.D., 1 do; Hatton Turner, Esq., R. E., 1 do; Smithsonian In- 


stitute, Washington, D. C., 1 do; Rey. C. Gray, 1 do; in all 29 
volumes. The Library has been re-arranged during the year, and 
now numbers 1,449 volumes, being for circulation 1,165; for refer- 
ence 954. It-is exceedingly useful as it is, yet the Committee is of 
opinion that certain additions might wisely be made to it. 


THE COMMITTEE. 

This Committee is now in a form in which it is hoped it may 
carry out better than ever its share of the work of the Association. 
Its Corresponding Members in the various Churches, if chosen from 
those who have the good of the Association at heart, will be able 
actively to canvass the young men of their acquaintance, and by an 
annual visit, to sustain their interest. in our organization. The 
efficiency of the Committee has been much crippled during the past 
year by circumstances which led to two changes in the Chairmanship. 


MISSION COMMITTEE. 
COTTAGE MEETINGS. 


The first work of this Committee was the organization of Cot- 
tage Meetings, four of which were established in December, besides 
the Sabbath eyening Meeting in Nazareth Street, Griffintown,—and 
these were in Colborne Avenue and Papineau Road, Quebec Suburbs, 
St. Constant Street, St. Lawrence Suburbs, and Prince Street, 
Griffintown. These Meetings were sustained for the winter months 
with undiminished numbers and interest, and cases of conversion in 
some of them much encouraged the workers. , 


SAILORS’ TRACT DISTRIBUTORS. 


This agency was entered. upon at the opening of the navigation, 
under the leadership of Mr. 'T. C. Jones, who reports the following 
figures :— |

Among the labourers who have been most constant during the 
year he mentions Messrs. Taylor, Topley, Charles Woodley, and 
Polievka. French tracts were scarce and foreign have not been 
much needed. The whole supply has been very carefully husbanded, 
making the figures, of course, much less than they might have been- 

Mr. Miuxen, our Missionary, divided his work during last 
winter, between his usual house-to-house visitation, visits to public 
institutions, and visiting in connection with Cottage Meetings, and 
the attendance on the bestowal of out-door relief at the iid of 
Refuge. His presence there not only greatly assists those in charge 
but serves to guide him to those places where his counsels are most 
needed. When spring opened the work among the seamen com- 
menced, and the Bethel service has since been maintained, with very 
encouraging attendance not only of sailors, but of crowds on shore, 
who listened attentively to the preaching of the Gospel. He now 
returns to his winter labours. The Sabbath morning service in the 
hospital is carried on by the Association through Mr. Millen. The 
following is a summary of his labours for the year :—

Mr. MILLEN, in his reports often renews his complaints against 
his old and untiring enemy—strong drink. 


THE MISSION COMMITTEE. 


This Committe has been led during the year by Mr. Cusutna. 
In their closing report they inform us that they think 60 at least can 
be well employed in the Cottage Meeting work this winter; they also 
recommend the employment as soon as possible of another Missionary. 


The Catholic Mission work of the city being now left entirely to 
this Association, it is evident that if there be any room for such 
labours at all, that the field is too large for one man, and Mr. MILLEN 
has always regarded the eastern section of the city as his sphere. 
That there is ever abundant need for such labourers as have no cause 


to build up, save Christ’s Kingdom, and whose efforts.can awaken no. 


sectarian prejudices is, we believe, the opinion of all who know the 
wants of our poor. 


COMMITTEE ON LECTURES, CLASSES AND MEETINGS. 
LECTURES. 

Shortly before this Committee entered upon its duties, it had 
been decided ‘to establish a course of free Lectures at the Rooms, to 
be delivered by clergymen and others. Your Committee endeavored, 
as far as possible, to carry out this design, and accordingly four 
lectures were given during the past winter, viz:—On November 
27th, 1866, by Rev. J. M. Gibson, subject “Galileo, the Astronomer ;”’ 
on December 18th, 1866, Rev. Dr. Wilkes, ‘‘ Formation of Habits ;” 
on February 5th, 1867, Mr. P. H. Burton, ‘‘The Old and the 
New;” on March 19th, 1867, Rev. D. H. Macviear, ‘ Rationalism.” 
All these lectures were attended by a large number of young men. 
Rev. Newman Hall also lectured before the Association in the Erskine 
Church, when that edifice was filled to its utmost capacity. 

There have also been two papers read, viz : By Mr. D. Matthews, 
on “Time and its Proper Use’; also, by Mr. R. T. Thomas, of 
Toronto, on a similar subject. 


CLASSES. 


The Literary Class, under the Presidency of Rev. Dr. Irvine, 
continued its meetings from the time your Committee was elected 
until the month of April, when it adjourned for the summer months. 
It again reorganized on Friday, the 18th October, when Rey. Dr. 
Hamilton.was elected President. The prospects thus far are very 
favorable that a goodly. number will attend.its meetings. 

The French Class was discontinued in March, and has not been 
reorganized, The advisability of forming a similar Class for 
the coming winter will doubtless be considered by the incoming 
Committee. 

Dr. Dawson’s Bible Class continued its session during the 
winter months, and was very largely attended. The subject chosen 


8 


for its study was “‘Some Passages in the Life and Character of Jesus 
Christ.” This Class was reorganized on Sabbath the 20th instant. 
It is designed to confine it exclusively to young men, and the subject 
for discussion is an “ Introduction to the Study of Prophecy,” 
the portion of Scripture chosen being the first chapters of Revela- 
tion. The meetings hitherto have been crowded, and the lessons 
exceedingly interesting. 


MEETINGS. 


During the year there have been held thirty-six weekly devo- 
tional meetings and twelve business meetings, only two meetings in 
the year having failed for lack of a quorum. We have been 
favoured several times with the presence of clergymen of the city, 
and frequently the visits of Ministers and others from elsewhere 
have been a ‘source of encouragement. The meetings have been 
attended, on the whole, as they never were before. One point of 
much importance is to be noted in connection with them,—namely, 
that the larger number of those present are always strangers, many 
of whom visit us once or twice and then come back no more, and 
some are touched by the spirit of God, and join themselves 
tous. No less than five young men have given their hearts to the 
Lord through the influence of these meetings during the last six 
weeks, besides these there may be others of whom we know nothing. 
To enable those who attend to become better acquainted with one 
another, the system of having an intermission of ten minutes for 
mutual introduction and private conversation has been lately adopted, 
with excellent results. 

A Sabbath afternoon Prayer Meeting was established shortly 
after the Convention, and has continued to meet up to the present. 
The meetings are large, and the Chairman, Mr. Grafton, reports 
them as being specially interesting. 

A daily Union Prayer Meeting was organized on July 1st, 
meeting at 12.30, and continuing for one hour. At first this meet- 
ing was well attended, but gradually the numbers decreased, and 
for some weeks past there have been times when but two or three 
‘were present. 

Day of Prayer.—In accordance with the appointment of the 
Convention, Sunday, November 10th, with the week following, has 
been appointed for special prayer for a blessing on Young Men’s 
Christian Associations, and the Cleregymen have been requested to 
address their congregations on the advantages and work of these 


Associations. It is hoped that the results of this appointment may 
be as good as all felt them to be last year. 


THE ANNUAL FESTIVAL. 


The Festival was held on the 14th of February, in Nordheimer’s 
Hall, and was presided over by Mr. Claxton. The speakers were 
the Rev. Mr. Sullivan, Rev. Drs. Jenkins and Major General Russell, 
K. C. B. Music was supplied by the Band of the 25th Regiment, 
and supper was served in an adjoining hall, which was tastefully 
decorated for the occasion. 


ASSISTANT SECRETARY'S LABOURS. 


Mr. Sandham spends his time in aiding in every department of 
the work, but in his special sphere of Missionary to young men, he 
has a great and good work on his hands; the following Summary is 
from his own Report :— 


“During the year that has passed, I have had many opportunities 
of aiding young men in various ways, and at the same time dropping 
a few words for Jesus, which [ hope have resulted in good to some.

It is suggested that the Assistant Secretary as Missionary to young 
men, be hereafter more closely associated with the Membership Com- 
mittee, whose work can ill be carried on without his assistance. 


CONVENTION. 3 
The repeated invitation presented to the members of sister 
societies to hold a Convention in Montreal having been at last ac- 
cepted by the Convention assembled in Albany last year, the 12th 
B 


10 


Annual Convention of the Young Men’s Christian Associations of 
the United States and British Provinces, was duly convened in this 
city on Wednesday, the 19th June, and continued its sessions until 
the afternoon of Sunday, 23rd June. The work of preparation for 
this great meeting was in the first instance given into the hands of a 
provisional committee who were directed to take all steps necessary 
in the meanwhile to the success of the meeting. This Committee, 
with the concurrence of the Association, sent invitations to a number 
of clergymen of note in. Britain, and to Mr. W. Edwyn Shipton of 
the London Association, to be present at the meeting at our charge. 
In due time they likewise invited a large number of ministers and 
eminent laymen from the States who were believed to have our cause 
at heart. They also issued sundry circulars and maintained needful 
correspondence with the Central Committee in New York. When 
the time of the meeting approached there were associated with the 
former three, namely, Messrs. Claxton, Bentley and Dougall, as 
Permanent Committee, a large number of the members to take 
up various departments of the work, the following being the 
names :—Messrs. Ross, Filer, Richards, Turnbull, Cushing, Holland, 
Middlemiss, Bazin, Court, James, Murphy, Young, Cameron, War- 
nock. 

The following gentlemen also consented to act as an Honorary 
Reception Committee :— Major-General Russell, K. C. B., Hon. Jas. 
Ferrier, Principal Dawson, L L.D., Messrs. HE. K. Greene, H. 
McLennan, James Court, Henry Lyman, and others. 

For the order of the meetings and the share taken in them by 
members of this Association, it is only necessary here to refer to the 
published proceedings of the Convention. In adopting the final 
report of the Convention Committee, votes of thanks were passed 
by the Association to all who had in any way contributed to its 
success. 

Besides the cheering information which has come to us in 
various ways from many parts of the continent, of the new zeal in- 
fused into many associations and the formation of new associations, 
we have experienced what we know, is only a small share of the 
benefit ourselves, but every day convinces us more and more of the 
reality of the blessing flowing to our Association both in its organi- 
zation and in its members. Our members, our meetings and our 
pecuniary support have greatly increased above anything we ever had 
before. 


li 


NEW ASSOCIATIONS. 


Point Str. CHARLES BRANCH ASSOCIATION. 


In the month of December the project of forming a Branch 
Association at Point St. Charles was laid before the Committee and 
by it committed to the Membership Committee, who with the con- 
currence of the General Committee appointed Messrs. Cushing, 
Dougall and Dredge, to carry out the design. In a short time an 
Association was formed and applied to the General Committee to 
know on what terms it might be admitted as a branch of the Mon- 
treal Association. In reply to this the following By-laws applicable 
to the circumstances, were adopted :— 


I.—Branches of this Association may be formed subject to the approval 
of the General Committee of this Association, by any number of Christian 
Young Men, not less than seven of whom shall be members of this Associ- 
ation. Such Branches and their members shall be subject to the Consti- 
tution of this Association. 

II—Not less than seven active members shall form a quorum at the 
business meetings of any such Branch. 

III.—The members of such Branches shall be members to all intents 
and purposes of this Association. 

IV.—Such Branches shall have power to elect members. 

V.—Branches shall report to the General Committee at least quarterly, 
and whensoever the said Committee shall require. 

VI.—Such Branches shall organize themselves under officers and by-laws 
in such manner as to them may seem fit. 

VII.—AIl moneys collected by such Branch Association, from member- 
ship subscriptions, or otherwise, shall be deposited with the Treasurer of 
the Montreal Association. The Montreal Association shall be responsible 
for the expenses of such Branches, provided such expenses be approved of 
by the General Committee. 

VIII.—One Delegate from each of such Branch Associotions shall 
occupy a seat on the General Committee of this Association. 


The words “in this city” were also, in due form struck from 
Article No. 2 of the Constitution. These provisions were accepted 
by the Point St. Charles Association, which thereby beeame a branch 
of this Association under the name of “The Point St. Charles 
Branch of the Montreal Young Men’s Christian Association,’ and in 
accordance with one of these the General Committee has received the 
following Annual Report from it :— 


12 


First ANNUAL REpoRT 
OF THE 
POINT ST. CHARLES BRANCH OF THE “MONTREAL 
YOUNG MEN’S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.” 


A public meeting, called by advertisement, was held in Point 
St. Charles on the 20th December, 1866, for the purpose of taking 
such steps as might be necessary for the organization of a Young 
Men’s Christian Association. The attendance was large, and it was 
resolved to ascertain what provision was, or could be made, to organize 
as a Branch of the Montreal Association. Pending these investiga- 
tions the Constitution of the Montreal Association was adopted and 
the following office-bearers elected for the ensuing year :— 


President—LEMUEL CUSHING, Jr. 
Vice-Presidents—WM. DICKSON ann JOHN McKERGOW. 
Seeretary-Treasurer—ROBT. McGLAUGHLIN. 
Committee—Messrs. AKIN, MATTHEWS, HORSFALL ann SMITH. 


A Committee was appointed to meet with the officers of the 
Montreal Association, and on the 7th January, 1867, this Committee 
submitted as the result of their labours a draft of By-Laws prepared 
by them with the assistance and co-operation of the General Com- 
mittee of the Montreal Association. Their Report was adopted and 
the organization of the Point St. Charles as a Branch of the “ Mon- 
treal Young Men’s Christian Association” was completed. 

A room was generously placed at the disposal of the Branch 
Association by T. Jas. Claxton, Esq., newspapers, magazines and other 
periodicals were obtained for the use of the members. A mutual 
improvement class was organized under the auspices of the Branch 
Association, meeting regularly in its rooms once a week. The meet- 
ings of the Association and its literary class were sustained through- 
out the winter months, and on the 3rd June, 1867, the room was 
closed for the summer to be re-opened in September. Owing to the 
absence of the President and other causes it was deemed advisable to 
delay the re-opening of the Rooms of the Branch Association until 
the 24th day of October last, when at a meeting called it was resolved 
to hold a social meeting on the 30th October. This last meeting was 
well attended. Resolutions were passed for renting and fitting up a 
more commodious and central room, and every indication was mani- 
fested of a vigorous prosecution of the enterprise thus far sustained 
and carried on with such apparent success. 


13 


KINGSTON AND BROCKVILLE ASSOCIATIONS. 


On the 25th of February of the present year certain members 
of this Association, namely, Messrs. Claxton, Cushing and Dougall, 
received an invitation to assist at the formation of an Association in 
Kingston. These, accompanied by Mr. Dredge, on reaching King- 
ston found that a public meeting had been called to receive them. 
A successful meeting was held in the hall attached to St. George’s 
Cathedral in that city, and a collection set on foot next morning to 
assist in the furnishing of rooms. A large number of zealous young 
men had been enlisted in the work, and the Committee is glad to 
learn that the Association there formed has thus far prospered. 
A similar meeting was held for a like purpose on the first of the 
present month in Brockville, which was attended by Messrs. Claxton, 
Bentley, Dredge and Richards, also by the Rev. Mr. Alexander of 
this city, and which resulted in the organization of an Association 
in that town with the happiest prospects of success. 


FINANCES. 

Mr. Burton, who was elected Treasurer at the last annual meet- 
ing had almost immediately to resign that office, and the Committee 
was forced to fall back upon the Society’s old Treasurer, Mr. Ross, 
who performed the duties of Treasurer while retaining the position 
of Vice-President. Mr. Claxton was Chairman of the Committee. 
The Treasurer’s statement herewith speaks for itself. The Finance 
Committee found the Association over $1,000 in debt, and close 
the year with a balance on hand. 

Shortly after the close of the Convention three liberal and hand- 
some subscriptions of $500 each were proffered to the Association, 
conditionally, that a building should be erected for their use ; after 
careful enquiry and some canvassing the conclusion was arrived at 
that the time had not yet come for us to undertake that much needed 
work. We may hope the day will soon come when we may claim 
these subscriptions, and have, as in other important cities, Rooms of 
our own, presented by the liberality of the wealthy merchants of this 
the chief city of the Dominion of Canada. 

The whole respectfully submitted, 


J. REDPATH DOUGALL, 


Secretary. 


MontTreaz, November 5th, 1867.
